intro: This guide covers **argument** questions: the one-paragraph arguments in each verbal section. Each topic gives the big idea, walks through one full question, then shows short examples with the right answer and the wrong answers that look right. Your weakest topic comes first, based on your own mocks.

formats.title: Argument (critical reasoning)
rules: Read the question line first, so you know what you're hunting for: something the author assumes, something that weakens, and so on. Watch for **EXCEPT** and **least**, which flip the job.
Before you look at the choices, finish this sentence in your head: *"the author is taking for granted that…"*
Every choice counts as true. Ask only what it does to the conclusion, not whether it's realistic.
On a select-all question, judge each choice on its own. There's no partial credit.

pacing: About **1:30 per argument**. Use the time to name the gap; rushing past that step is where misses come from.
At **2:30** with two choices left, pick the one that touches the gap, mark it, and move on.

sections.title: Assumptions (what the argument needs)
sections.idea: An assumption is something the author needs to be true but never says. Look for what the conclusion talks about that the evidence never showed. To check a choice, flip it to its opposite: if the argument falls apart, the author needed it.

example.q: A transit authority plans to replace each diesel bus with an electric one as the diesel wears out. Electric buses cost more to buy, but the authority says the fuel savings will more than make up for it over the **twelve years a bus typically stays in service**. The plan assumes which of the following? (A) *Electric buses are quieter than diesel buses.* (B) *The price of electricity will not rise at any point in the next twelve years.* (C) *Electric buses will stay in service about as long as the diesel buses they replace.*
steps: The savings only pay off over twelve years, and twelve years is how long the **diesel** buses last. Nothing says an electric bus lasts that long.
Flip (C): electric buses wear out after six years. Now the authority buys two for every diesel, and the savings vanish. The argument falls apart, so (C) is the answer.

Flip (B): electricity gets a bit pricier at some point. Electric buses can still come out cheaper, so the argument survives. (B) asks for far more than the plan needs. Words like *never*, *all* and *at any point* are a warning sign on assumption questions.
(A) may well be true, but the argument is about **cost**. Noise is a different topic.

examples.q: "Fewer speeding tickets since the new signs went up, so the signs slowed drivers down."
examples.label: Assumed
examples.answer: police weren't writing fewer tickets for some other reason, like fewer patrols.

wrong.text: No driver has sped on that road since the signs went up.
wrong.why: Too strong. The argument says drivers slowed down, not that every single one did. Flip it (a few still speed) and the argument is fine.

wrong.text: Speeding causes most crashes on that road.
wrong.why: Explains why the signs matter, but the conclusion is about whether drivers slowed, not about crashes.

examples.q: "Two farms that put up perches for hawks now have fewer mice. If every farm in the valley put up perches, mice would drop everywhere."
examples.label: Assumed
examples.answer: the valley has enough hawks to use all the new perches.

wrong.text: Every farm will see the same drop in mice as the first two.
wrong.why: Too strong. The conclusion only says mice would drop, not by the same amount.

wrong.text: Hawks eat more mice than any other bird.
wrong.why: Sounds related, but whether owls eat more doesn't matter. Flip it and the perches can still work.

examples.q: "Students wait a long time to use the library's computers, so adding ten more computers will cut the wait."
examples.label: Assumed
examples.answer: students wait because there aren't enough computers, not because of something else, like a slow sign-in system.

wrong.text: The new computers are faster than the old ones.
wrong.why: A nice extra, but not needed. If the problem was too few computers, more of them helps even at the same speed.

wrong.text: Every student will get a computer right away.
wrong.why: Too strong. The plan only claims the wait will be shorter, not gone.

sections.title: Weaken & strengthen
sections.idea: The facts are true; you're judging whether they lead to the conclusion. To **weaken**, show the facts could happen even if the conclusion is wrong, usually because something else explains them. To **strengthen**, rule that something else out. A strong-sounding choice is fine here: it just means a bigger effect.

example.q: After Route 9 got new, quieter buses, ridership rose 30 percent. The transit office concludes that riders like the new buses. Which most weakens this? (A) *Most new riders used to drive to work.* (B) *At the same time, Route 9 started running twice as often.* (C) *The new buses cost more than the old ones.*
steps: The office says the **buses** caused the rise. Ask: what else changed?
(B): buses coming twice as often could bring in riders on its own. That's another cause, so it weakens.
(A) says where the riders came from, not **why** they came. It sounds relevant but changes nothing.
(C) is about the city's budget, not about why riders showed up.

examples.q: "People who own exercise bikes are fitter than people who don't, so buying one will make you fitter."
examples.label: Weakens
examples.answer: people usually buy an exercise bike after they've already started getting fit. The fitness may come first.

wrong.text: Exercise bikes are expensive.
wrong.why: Price says nothing about whether the bike makes you fit.

wrong.text: Running outdoors burns more calories than an exercise bike.
wrong.why: The claim is that the bike helps, not that it's the best workout.

examples.q: "Towns with more coffee shops have higher incomes, so opening coffee shops raises a town's income."
examples.label: Weakens
examples.answer: coffee chains choose to open in towns where people already earn more. Wealth brings the shops, not the other way around.

wrong.text: Coffee shops hire many local workers.
wrong.why: Wrong direction: more local jobs would **support** the claim.

wrong.text: A few wealthy towns have almost no coffee shops.
wrong.why: A few exceptions don't break a pattern that holds across most towns.

examples.q: "To cut litter in its parks, the city will fine anyone caught dropping trash 200 dollars."
examples.label: Weakens
examples.answer: the city has two officers to patrol fifty parks, so almost no one will be caught.

wrong.text: Many residents think a 200-dollar fine is too harsh.
wrong.why: Whether people find it fair doesn't tell you if litter drops. A scary fine may even work better.

wrong.text: Litter in the parks has risen for five years.
wrong.why: This shows the problem is real, which makes the plan look more needed, not less likely to work.

examples.q: "After a college made first-year math pass/fail, more first-years kept taking math. The college credits the new grading."
examples.label: Strengthens
examples.answer: similar colleges that kept letter grades saw no rise in first-years staying in math over the same years. That rules out a wider trend, like more interest in math everywhere or easier classes everywhere, that could explain the rise without pass/fail.

wrong.text: Students say they prefer pass/fail grading.
wrong.why: This shows students like the policy, not that it actually kept them in math.

wrong.text: Students who stayed in math later earned more.
wrong.why: This shows staying in math paid off later. It doesn't show that pass/fail is what made them stay.

sections.title: Flaws & evaluate questions
sections.idea: A **flaw** question asks you to name the author's mistake. It's the same gap as an assumption, described as an error: *"takes for granted that…"*, *"fails to consider…"*. An **evaluate** question asks what you'd most want to find out. The right answer is a question where one answer helps the argument and the other hurts it.

example.q: Remote workers at a firm closed 20 percent more support tickets than office workers last year, so the manager concludes that working from home makes people more productive. Which would be most useful to know? (A) *Whether remote workers were given easier tickets.* (B) *Whether office workers would also like to work from home.* (C) *Whether the firm plans to hire more remote workers.*
steps: The gap: more tickets only means more productive if the tickets were equally hard.
Answer (A) both ways. Yes, easier tickets: that explains the gap, so the argument is weaker. No: the comparison is fair, so it's stronger. Either answer matters, so (A) is right.
(B): yes or no, what office workers want says nothing about productivity.
(C): a future plan doesn't tell you whether last year's numbers mean what the manager thinks.

examples.q: "In a survey of a running magazine's readers, most said they exercise six days a week. So most adults in the country exercise almost daily."
examples.label: Flaw
examples.answer: it draws a conclusion about all adults from a group that is probably far more active than most.

wrong.text: It relies on people's own reports of how much they exercise.
wrong.why: A smaller problem. Even perfectly honest answers would still come only from runners.

wrong.text: It assumes the magazine's readers enjoy running.
wrong.why: Whether they enjoy it doesn't matter, and the argument never claims it.

examples.q: "No study has shown that the new sweetener is harmful, so it must be safe."
examples.label: Flaw
examples.answer: it treats a lack of proof that something is harmful as proof that it's safe.

wrong.text: It relies on studies paid for by the sweetener's maker.
wrong.why: The argument doesn't cite any studies, so it can't rely on them.

wrong.text: It mistakes a cause for an effect.
wrong.why: Real flaw wording, but nothing in this argument is a cause and effect.

examples.q: "You need a passing test score to join the team. Maya passed, so she'll make the team."
examples.label: Flaw
examples.answer: it treats something you **need** to join as if it were **enough** to join.

wrong.text: It assumes Maya's score was high.
wrong.why: The argument only uses that she passed. How high doesn't come up.

wrong.text: It draws a general rule from one person.
wrong.why: There's no general rule here; it's only about Maya.

examples.q: "Last year, 60 percent of the store's complaints were about its app, up from 20 percent the year before. So the app is causing more problems than ever."
examples.label: Flaw
examples.answer: it reads a bigger **share** as a bigger **number**. If total complaints fell from 100 to 30, app complaints went from 20 to 18.

wrong.text: It assumes every complaint was fair.
wrong.why: Fair or not, the mistake is in how the numbers are read.

wrong.text: It ignores customers who like the app.
wrong.why: Happy customers don't change how many complaints there were.

sections.title: Paradoxes (explain the surprise)
sections.idea: Two facts seem to clash. Don't argue with either one. The answer is a new fact that lets **both** be true at once.

example.q: Lakeside Hospital has the highest-rated surgeons in the state, yet its patients die after surgery more often than at any other hospital. Which best explains this? (A) *Lakeside's surgeons are not as skilled as their ratings suggest.* (B) *Doctors across the state send their riskiest cases to Lakeside.* (C) *Lakeside has more surgeons than any other hospital.*
steps: The clash: the best surgeons should lose fewer patients, but they lose more.
(B): if Lakeside gets the hardest cases, more of its patients die even with great surgeons. Both facts stand, so (B) is right.
(A) says one of the facts is wrong. A paradox answer never does that.
(C): more surgeons means more operations, but the clash is about the death **rate**, which size doesn't explain.

examples.q: "The city cut bus fares in half, but its income from fares went **up**."
examples.label: Explains
examples.answer: so many new riders joined that the total collected rose, even at the lower price.

wrong.text: Many riders had complained that the old fares were too high.
wrong.why: Explains why the city cut fares, not why income rose. Only one side of the clash.

wrong.text: The cost of running the buses also went up.
wrong.why: Costs aren't income; this doesn't touch the clash at all.

examples.q: "After a ski resort put up better safety nets, injuries on its slopes went **up**."
examples.label: Explains
examples.answer: feeling safer, skiers started taking steeper runs at higher speeds.

wrong.text: The nets were expensive to install.
wrong.why: Cost says nothing about why injuries rose.

wrong.text: Most injuries at the resort are minor.
wrong.why: That's about how bad the injuries are, not why there are more of them.

sections.title: Boldface, main point & completing the argument
sections.idea: Find the **main conclusion** first: the claim everything else is there to support. Then each other part is either for it, against it, or background. For a fill-in-the-blank, the blank after *since* or *because* needs a reason that backs up the claim before it.

example.q: Some experts predict that a new bridge toll will push drivers onto side streets. **But most bridge trips are commutes with no practical detour.** Therefore, **the toll is unlikely to shift much traffic.** What roles do the two bold parts play? (A) *The first is evidence for the main conclusion; the second is that conclusion.* (B) *The first is the main conclusion; the second is evidence for it.* (C) *The first is a view the argument opposes; the second is the main conclusion.*
steps: *Therefore* marks the second bold part. It's the author's own point: the **main conclusion**.
The first bold part comes after *But* and gives a reason the toll won't shift traffic. It's **evidence for** the conclusion. So (A) is right.
(B) has the right labels on the wrong parts.
(C) is half right. The view the argument opposes is the experts' prediction, which isn't in bold. One wrong half sinks the whole choice.

examples.q: "Our library is packed every evening, so it clearly needs more space. The council should approve the new wing." What is the main conclusion?
examples.label: Main conclusion
examples.answer: The council should approve the new wing.

wrong.text: The library needs more space.
wrong.why: It's backed up by the first fact, but then it's used to back up the vote. A middle step, not the main point.

wrong.text: The library is packed every evening.
wrong.why: That's the evidence everything starts from.

examples.q: "Although the new phone has a smaller battery, it lasts longer than last year's, because its chip uses much less power." What role does the smaller battery play?
examples.label: Role
examples.answer: a point against the conclusion that the author admits, then outweighs.

wrong.text: Evidence for the conclusion.
wrong.why: A smaller battery makes a longer life harder, not easier.

wrong.text: The main conclusion.
wrong.why: The main point is that the phone lasts longer; the battery is just conceded.

examples.q: "Many people think online classes will replace lecture halls. That's unlikely, since ___."
examples.label: Completes it
examples.answer: most students say they learn better when they can ask questions face to face.

wrong.text: online classes are cheaper for colleges to run.
wrong.why: Wrong direction: this makes replacement **more** likely.

wrong.text: every college will keep at least one lecture hall forever.
wrong.why: Goes far beyond *unlikely*. It also just restates the claim instead of giving a reason.
